segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I, Paul, appeal to you myself, by the gentleness and forbearance of Christ—I who am lowly when face to face among you, but bold toward you when away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I beg you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence I reckon on daring to use against certain people, who reckon that we walk according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but powerful through God for the tearing down of strongholds—we tear down reasonings

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we stand ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look at what is right in front of your face. If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him reckon this again for himself: just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be put to shame.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not want to seem as though I were trying to frighten you through my letters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “His letters,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: someone says,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech counts for nothing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let such a person reckon this: what we are in word through letters when absent, we also are in deed when present.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are without understanding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the sphere that God apportioned to us as our measure, to reach even as far as you—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we are not overstretching ourselves, as though we did not reach you, since we came even as far as you with the good news of Christ—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: we do not boast beyond measure in the labors of others, but we have hope that, as your faith grows, we will be greatly enlarged among you in keeping with our sphere,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so as to proclaim the good news in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in what is already done in another's sphere.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

notes.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, unassertive manner, and 'gentleness' is the mainstream modern rendering. The paired word, rendered 'forbearance', was often used of the leniency of someone with the power to be severe.

Paul appears to be echoing a charge made by his critics in Corinth (see verse 10): that he is unimpressive and submissive in person and bold only from a distance. In ordinary Greek usage the word was often unflattering, meaning low in status or servile.

Paul plays on two phrases. To walk 'in the flesh' (verse 3) is simply to live as an ordinary mortal human being. To walk or wage war 'according to the flesh' is to act by merely human standards and motives. 'Walk' is a Semitic idiom for how one conducts one's life.

The Greek is literally 'powerful to God', and its force is disputed. It may mean powerful by God's enabling (as rendered here), powerful in God's service, powerful in God's sight, or it may be a Semitic idiom meaning 'supremely powerful'. Translations and commentators are divided.

Verses 4–6 follow the sequence of an ancient siege: fortifications are torn down, raised defences are levelled, the defenders are taken captive, and remaining resistance is punished. Paul applies the picture to arguments and ways of thinking opposed to the knowledge of God.

notes.phrase: Look at what is right in front of your face.
notes.traditional: Do ye look on things after the outward appearance?
notes.note: The Greek verb form can be a command ('Look at what is in front of you'), a statement ('You are looking only at the surface of things') or a question. Many modern translations take it as a command, as here; others take it as a rebuke for judging by appearances. The phrase 'in front of your face' picks up 'face to face' in verse 1.

The Greek verb is singular, 'he says' or 'one says'. It may refer to a particular critic or be an impersonal way of reporting what is generally being said; some manuscripts have the plural 'they say'. 'Such a person' in verse 11 is equally open to either reading.

A few manuscripts of the Western tradition lack these words and the opening 'We, however' of verse 13. In that form of the text it is Paul and his colleagues who measure themselves by their own standard. The longer reading translated here is much better attested and is followed by nearly all editions.

The Greek word basically means a measuring rod, and hence a standard or limit. Here and in verses 15–16 most interpreters take it to mean the area of mission work God marked out for Paul, which is why it is rendered 'sphere'. Others understand it as the standard by which his work is to be assessed. The sentence is compressed and its exact sense is debated.

'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'; the related verb in verse 16 is rendered 'proclaim the good news'.

notes.phrase: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”
notes.note: This is a condensed quotation of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Septuagint), where the one who boasts is told to boast in understanding and knowing the Lord. Paul gives no introductory formula here, but he cites the same words with 'as it is written' in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul with senses from physical body to merely human standards to sinful nature, and translations vary widely between 'flesh', 'human', 'worldly' and 'sinful nature'.
A key Pauline word group (with καύχημα, καύχησις) rendered variously as 'boast', 'glory', 'take pride' and 'rejoice'; readers lose the thread if it varies.
Central in Romans 4 and frequent elsewhere, rendered 'reckon', 'count', 'credit', 'consider' or 'think'; here Paul plays on it repeatedly, so a consistent choice matters.
The Semitic 'walk' idiom for conduct recurs across Paul and John; translations split between 'walk' and 'live', and a single policy is needed.
Self-commendation is a running theme in 2 Corinthians and the verb also occurs in Romans; 'commend', 'recommend' and 'demonstrate' compete.

patch.reason: euangelion promoted to active after full-run drift (good news 37 / gospel 35)
